wiki_excerpt:
Pewter () is a malleable metal alloy traditionally of tin and as much as 40% lead. In order to prevent lead poisoning modern pewter replaces lead with antimony (approximately 5–10%), copper (2%), bismuth, and sometimes silver. Pewter has a low melting point, around 170–230 °C (338–446 °F), depending on the exact mixture of metals. The word pewter is possibly a variation of "spelter", a term for zinc alloys (originally a colloquial name for zinc).


History
Pewter was first used around the beginning of the Bronze Age in the Near East. The earliest known piece of pewter was found in an Egyptian tomb, c. 1450 BC, but it is unlikely that this was the first use of the material. Pewter was used for decorative metal items and tableware in ancient times by the Egyptians and later the Romans, and came into extensive use in Europe from the Middle Ages until the various developments in pottery and glass-making during the 18th and 19th centuries. Pewter was a leading material for producing plates, cups, and bowls before the wide adoption of porcelain. Mass production of pottery, porcelain and glass products have almost universally replaced pewter in daily life, although pewter artifacts continue to be produced, mainly as decorative or specialty items. Pewter was also used around East Asia. Pewter was used for household items in Roman Britain, particularly in the south of the country.
Lidless mugs and lidded tankards may be the most familiar pewter artifacts from the late 17th and 18th centuries, although the metal was also used for many other items including porringers (shallow bowls), plates, dishes, basins, spoons, measures, flagons, communion cups, teapots, sugar bowls, beer steins (tankards), and cream jugs. In the early 19th century, changes in fashion caused a decline in the use of pewter flatware. At the same time, production increased of both cast and spun pewter tea sets, whale-oil lamps, candlesticks, and so on. Later in the century, pewter alloys were often used as a base metal for silver-plated objects.
In the late 19th century, pewter came back into fashion with the revival of medieval objects for decoration. New replicas of medieval pewter objects were created, and collected for decoration. Today, pewter is used in decorative objects, mainly collectible statuettes and figurines, game figures, aircraft and other models, (replica) coins, pendants, plated jewellery and so on. Certain athletic contests, such as the United States Figure Skating Championships, award pewter medals to fourth-place finishers.


Types
In antiquity, pewter was tin alloyed with lead and sometimes also copper. Older pewters with higher lead content are heavier, tarnish faster, and their oxidation has a darker, silver-gray color. Pewters containing lead are no longer used in items that will come in contact with food or the human body (such as cups, plates, or jewelry), due to the toxicity of lead. grok_lead: Pewter is a malleable, tin-based metal alloy primarily composed of 85â99% tin, with smaller amounts of antimony (typically 1â8%), copper (0.25â3%), and sometimes bismuth or silver, making it suitable for casting intricate designs and everyday items. Modern standards, such as ASTM B560, define pewter as lead-free to ensure safety, distinguishing it from historical formulations that included up to 40% lead. Its low melting point (around 170â230Â°C) and softness allow for easy working, while its bluish-white luster and resistance to tarnishing contribute to its enduring appeal in craftsmanship. Originating over 2,000 years ago in ancient Egypt and Rome, pewter was used for household vessels and decorative pieces, with evidence of Roman production dating to the 1st century CE. By the Middle Ages in Europe, particularly Britain, it gained prominence as an affordable alternative to silver, receiving ecclesiastical approval in 1074 for church vessels at the Synod of Rouen. The 17th and 18th centuries marked pewter's "Golden Age" in England, where guilds regulated its production, and it became a staple in affluent homes for tableware like tankards, plates, and spoons. In colonial America, pewter arrived with early settlers around 1630, serving as essential domestic ware despite the scarcity of tin, which was imported while local lead was abundant. Its popularity waned in the 19th century with the rise of ceramics, glass, and electroplated silver, but revival efforts in the 20th century emphasized lead-free compositions. Today, pewter remains valued for its versatility in both functional and ornamental applications, including jewelry, picture frames, candlesticks, and modern tableware, thanks to its non-toxic, lead-free formulations that comply with food safety standards. Artisans appreciate its castability for detailed sculptures and Art Nouveau-style pieces, while its durability and recyclability support sustainable manufacturing practices. Organizations like the Pewter Society continue to promote its cultural heritage through collections and education, ensuring pewter's role in contemporary design and historical preservation.
